records.title: Screening for Intimate Partner Violence and Caregiver Abuse of Older or Vulnerable Adults: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
records.design: guideline / recommendation statement (systematic-review-based)
records.population_setting: US adolescents and adults, pregnant/postpartum and reproductive-age women; older/vulnerable adults without recognized signs of abuse
records.key_finding: USPSTF concludes screening for IPV in women of reproductive age (including pregnant/postpartum), combined with provision or referral to multicomponent interventions, has moderate net benefit (B recommendation). For caregiver abuse/neglect of older or vulnerable adults, benefits and harms remain undetermined (I statement) even in this 2025 update.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly supports P5 (referral quality: timeliness, accessibility, follow-through) and the FAILURE CRITERION logic -- the global-guidance benefit is conditional on referral/intervention, not screening/knowledge alone; the persistent I-statement for vulnerable-adult abuse also cautions against assuming any T-PHE mechanism 'works' in undertested subpopulations.
records.evidence_level: Global guidance (USPSTF systematic-review-based recommendation, 2025 update)

records.title: Screening for Intimate Partner Violence, Elder Abuse, and Abuse of Vulnerable Adults: US Preventive Services Task Force Final Recommendation Statement
records.design: guideline / recommendation statement
records.population_setting: US women of reproductive age; older/vulnerable adults
records.key_finding: With moderate certainty, screening plus referral to ongoing support services has moderate net benefit; explicitly states evidence does NOT support the effectiveness of brief interventions or merely providing referral information in the absence of ongoing supportive intervention components, and that benefit evidence is concentrated in pregnant/postpartum populations.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly complicates P5/referral-quality claims and the STOP RULE's assumption that referral alone suffices -- explicit global-guidance evidence that a referral pamphlet/information-only pathway is not established as effective; supports the T-PHE emphasis on accountable, ongoing referral rather than a one-time hand-off.
records.evidence_level: Global guidance (USPSTF recommendation statement, moderate-certainty evidence)

records.title: Screening for intimate partner violence and abuse of elderly and vulnerable adults: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendation statement
records.design: guideline / recommendation statement
records.population_setting: US asymptomatic women of reproductive age; elderly and vulnerable adults
records.key_finding: First USPSTF B-grade recommendation to screen women of childbearing age for IPV and refer positive screens to intervention services, updating a 2004 insufficient-evidence (I) statement; evidence for elderly/vulnerable-adult screening remained insufficient (I statement).
records.relevance_to_tphe: Documents the evidence trajectory (2004 insufficient -> 2013 B -> 2018/2025 updates) that T-PHE's programme theory should be read against; supports treating IPV screening/referral guidance as an evolving, tier-honest evidence base rather than settled fact, consistent with the epistemic-humility safeguard.
records.evidence_level: Global guidance (USPSTF recommendation statement)

records.title: Screening for family and intimate partner violence: recommendation statement
records.design: guideline / recommendation statement
records.population_setting: US general population, family and intimate partner violence screening in primary care
records.key_finding: USPSTF found the evidence insufficient (I statement) to recommend for or against routine screening instruments to detect domestic violence, updating a 1996 insufficient-evidence finding; explicitly states the letter grade reflects the quality and magnitude of evidence available at that time, not an assumption of no benefit.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Historical baseline showing that even the narrow, well-resourced clinical screening literature took over a decade to accumulate evidence sufficient for a positive recommendation -- cautions against assuming a practitioner-led programme-theory synthesis like T-PHE has already crossed an analogous evidentiary threshold; relevant to epistemic humility (P1-adjacent) and the FAILURE CRITERION.
records.evidence_level: Global guidance (USPSTF recommendation statement, historical)

records.title: Screening women for intimate partner violence: a systematic review to update the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendation
records.design: systematic review (evidence base for USPSTF 2013 update)
records.population_setting: Women in health care settings, US-relevant evidence base
records.key_finding: Of 15 fair/good-quality studies evaluating 13 screening instruments, 6 were highly accurate; 14 studies found minimal adverse effects from screening, though some women reported discomfort, loss of privacy, emotional distress, and fear of further abuse; counseling interventions reduced IPV/improved outcomes in some subpopulations (pregnant women, new mothers, family-planning clients) but a large trial found no significant screening-vs-usual-care difference overall.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly relevant to the STOP RULE and dignity/consent safeguard: names concrete harm categories from disclosure (loss of privacy, emotional distress, fear of further abuse) that a joint-couple education format could plausibly worsen, supporting P4 (private/confidential channel and the stop rule for suspected coercion).
records.evidence_level: Systematic review underlying global guidance (USPSTF evidence report)

records.title: Screening women for intimate partner violence in healthcare settings
records.design: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 RCTs/quasi-RCTs (n=14,959)
records.population_setting: Women in antenatal, women's health, emergency department and primary care settings, mostly high-income urban settings
records.key_finding: Screening increased clinical identification of IPV victims (OR 2.95, 95% CI 1.79-4.87, n=10,074) but there was no evidence of effect on referrals to support services (OR 2.24, 95% CI 0.64-7.86, only 2 studies, n=1298), no evidence screening reduced women's re-exposure to violence at 3-18 months, and insufficient evidence on health outcomes or harm beyond the immediate post-screening period; authors conclude screening alone is insufficiently supported to justify universal implementation absent stronger referral/outcome evidence.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Core evidentiary anchor for the T-PHE FAILURE CRITERION and P2/P5: this is the canonical finding that identification/screening without demonstrated referral and downstream-outcome effect does not establish improved safety -- directly supports T-PHE's proposition that conventional 'success' (e.g., completion, knowledge) can coexist with failure on the substantive outcomes (coercion recognition, safe help-seeking, accountable referral).
records.evidence_level: global evidence (Cochrane systematic review, moderate-to-low certainty per outcome)

records.title: Psychological therapies for women who experience intimate partner violence
records.design: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of 33 RCTs (n=5517 women)
records.population_setting: Women aged 16+ with recent or lifetime IPV experience, mostly high-income countries, recruited from healthcare, community, shelter/refuge settings
records.key_finding: Psychological therapies probably reduce depression at medium-term follow-up (SMD -0.24, 95% CI -0.47 to -0.01; 4 trials, 600 women, moderate certainty) and may reduce anxiety, but evidence is uncertain or absent for self-efficacy, PTSD, re-exposure to IPV, and safety planning; harm data are limited (only 1 of 33 trials used a validated harm-outcome scale).
records.relevance_to_tphe: Relevant to P5/referral quality and the FAILURE CRITERION's mental-health-literacy domain: shows that even well-studied downstream interventions for IPV survivors have narrow, outcome-specific evidence and thin harm surveillance -- cautions against assuming any referral destination in T-PHE's pathway is automatically protective, reinforcing the need for the six safeguards rather than referral alone.
records.evidence_level: Global evidence (Cochrane systematic review, moderate-to-low certainty per outcome)

records.title: The health-systems response to violence against women
records.design: Series paper / narrative review with five country case studies
records.population_setting: Health systems in low-, middle- and high-income countries
records.key_finding: Reviews evidence for clinical interventions and health-system components (protocols, training, capacity-building) needed to identify and support women subjected to IPV/sexual violence following the 2013 WHO guidelines and 67th World Health Assembly resolution; finds substantial system and behavioural barriers to implementation, especially in low- and middle-income countries, and that system development has generally been slow.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Supports P5 (referral quality depends on system-level timeliness, accessibility, follow-through, not individual practitioner goodwill) and the bounded-authority/referral safeguard -- a WHO-aligned account of why referral pathways commonly fail in practice, directly relevant to the STOP RULE's assumption that a confidential assessment pathway will actually be accessible.
records.evidence_level: Global guidance-linked evidence synthesis (WHO-affiliated Lancet Series paper)

records.title: Integrating gender-based violence first-line response into family planning and antenatal care services: an assessment of feasibility, appropriateness and acceptability to healthcare providers in Sokoto and Ebonyi States, Nigeria
records.design: Mixed-methods implementation study embedded in a matched-pair cluster-controlled trial (75 providers, 20 facilities)
records.population_setting: Antenatal care and family planning clinics, Nigeria; nurse-midwives and community health extension workers trained in WHO LIVES + ARCHES
records.key_finding: Quality-assurance readiness scores for GBV first-line response increased significantly over 9 months (P<=0.05); providers rated integration as appropriate/acceptable (~3 of 4 on average) but reported it initially felt like added work, and lack of funds/staff was a key barrier; feasibility/acceptability pulse scores showed no significant change over time despite improved facility readiness.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly supports P5 (referral/response quality requires sustained investment, mentoring, and resourcing, not a one-off training) and complicates T-PHE's implicit assumption that a governance-layer safeguard can be added to existing practitioner workflows without resource cost -- relevant to bounded authority and repairability safeguards.
records.evidence_level: Global-guidance-aligned implementation evidence (WHO LIVES model), single-country mixed-methods study

records.title: Effectiveness of a clinic-based counselling intervention on risk of experiencing intimate partner violence and reproductive coercion: a matched-pair cluster-controlled trial in Ebonyi and Sokoto, Nigeria
records.design: Quasi-experimental matched-pair cluster-controlled trial (n=1617 clients, 20 intervention vs 20 comparison clinics)
records.population_setting: Family planning and antenatal care clients, Nigeria
records.key_finding: Combined WHO LIVES + ARCHES first-line response reduced relative risk of IPV exposure (beta=0.54, 95% CI 0.30-0.98) and reproductive coercion (beta=0.51, 95% CI 0.28-0.94) over 9 months among women not already experiencing violence, but showed no effect on modern contraceptive use; authors note LIVES and ARCHES individually have shown 'mixed effects' in prior trials.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Direct evidentiary anchor for the LIVES-based STOP RULE/first-line-response mechanism T-PHE invokes: shows a positive, quantified effect on IPV/coercion risk reduction from a structured first-line-response protocol delivered by trained clinic staff -- supports P2/P4 but the qualifier 'mixed effects' in prior trials and the null contraceptive-use finding are relevant caveats for the FAILURE CRITERION (a positive effect on one outcome does not guarantee effect on others).
records.evidence_level: primary evidence (cluster-controlled trial; effectiveness study, not systematic review)

records.title: Protocol for a matched-pair cluster control trial of ARCHES (Addressing Reproductive Coercion in Health Settings) among women and girls seeking contraceptive services from community-based clinics in Nairobi, Kenya
records.design: Trial protocol
records.population_setting: Women/girls seeking contraceptive services, community-based clinics, Nairobi, Kenya
records.key_finding: Describes ARCHES as a single-session, clinic-based enhanced counseling model that creates opportunity for patient disclosure of reproductive coercion/IPV followed by warm referral to local services; explicitly notes that to date, no clinic-based GBV intervention had been shown to reduce reproductive coercion or unintended pregnancy in LMIC settings, motivating this trial.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Supports P5's definition of referral quality via the concept of 'warm referral' (direct handoff rather than passive information) as the mechanism theorized to matter, but the stated absence of prior LMIC evidence of effect is a relevant limitation/gap for T-PHE's cultural-intelligibility safeguard (P3), since Thailand is itself an LMIC/upper-middle-income intercultural setting.
records.evidence_level: Global-guidance-aligned protocol (pre-registered trial design; no outcome data yet in this record)

records.title: Women's preferences for how health practitioners respond to coercive control by a partner: Open-ended survey qualitative analysis
records.design: Qualitative directed content analysis of open-ended survey responses (n=682 women with lived experience of coercive control)
records.population_setting: Australian women who had experienced coercive control
records.key_finding: Findings align with the WHO LIVES framework (Listen-Inquire-Validate-Enhance safety-Support) and the CARE framework (Choice and control-Action and advocacy-Recognition and understanding-Emotional connection); women wanted specific validating, non-judgmental scripted language from practitioners and messaging that counteracts coercive-controlling tactics rather than generic acknowledgement.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly supports P4 (dignity and consent safeguard) and the affected-person-visibility safeguard: patient-derived (not practitioner-derived) evidence on what a supportive first-line response should sound like, reinforcing that T-PHE's decision-control mechanism should be evaluated against what affected persons themselves report as helpful, not practitioner assumption.
records.evidence_level: Dr-tier qualitative evidence (patient-reported preferences, single high-income-country sample)

records.title: Housing interventions for women experiencing intimate partner violence: a systematic review
records.first_author: Baker CK / Sprague S (co-first authorship per abstract group)
records.design: Systematic review of 34 controlled quantitative studies (from 23,902 screened records)
records.population_setting: Women experiencing IPV, predominantly US-based housing/shelter programmes
records.key_finding: No cumulative evidence of disadvantage from any IPV-housing intervention; evidence of benefit was strongest for mental health outcomes, intent to leave partner, perceived safety, and reduced housing/partner-related stress; most included studies were at high risk of bias, and evidence for long-term/non-US housing solutions was sparse.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Relevant to P5/referral quality and repairability: illustrates that 'referral' is not a single endpoint but a continuum of downstream services (shelter through permanent housing) whose evidence quality varies -- supports treating referral fidelity/follow-through as a graded, not binary, safeguard, and flags a geographic gap (mostly USA) relevant to Thailand-specific applicability.
records.evidence_level: Global evidence (systematic review, high risk of bias in underlying studies per authors)

records.title: Consistency and sources of divergence in recommendations on screening with questionnaires for presently experienced health problems or symptoms: a comparison of recommendations from the Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care, UK National Screening Committee, and US Preventive Services Task Force
records.design: Comparative methodological review of guideline organizations (includes IPV screening as one of 22 compared recommendations)
records.population_setting: Cross-national comparison of screening guideline bodies (Canada, UK, US)
records.key_finding: Among 22 questionnaire-based screening recommendations compared across three major guideline bodies (including IPV screening), recommendations diverged substantially, and direct RCT evidence for the effectiveness of the questionnaire-based screening itself (as opposed to downstream treatment) was often absent or indirect.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Supports the epistemic-humility safeguard (P1-adjacent) directly: even at the level of global, authoritative task forces, screening recommendations for conditions including IPV are not uniform and are frequently built on indirect rather than direct RCT evidence -- a caution against T-PHE or any programme theory over-claiming certainty from guideline citation alone.
records.evidence_level: Global guidance meta-comparison (methodological review across USPSTF/UKNSC/CTFPHC)

records.title: The anatomy of a community health center system-level intervention for intimate partner violence
records.design: 3-year community-based participatory mixed-methods demonstration project across 4 community health centers
records.population_setting: Urban, predominantly indigent safety-net primary care population, USA
records.key_finding: Implementing USPSTF-guideline-consistent universal IPV screening and referral in resource-limited urban primary care settings faced significant system-level challenges (workflow, staff capacity, referral infrastructure), even with a dedicated multi-year system-level intervention designed to raise detection and response.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Supports P5 and the bounded-authority/referral safeguard: concrete evidence that translating a screening/referral mandate into functioning practice requires sustained system-level investment, directly analogous to the resourcing gap risk in T-PHE's referral pathway for premarital couples in resource-constrained community settings.
records.evidence_level: Dr-tier implementation evidence (single-country participatory demonstration project)

records.title: Effect of domestic violence training: systematic review of randomized controlled trials
records.first_author: Waalen J (per Can Fam Physician synthesis authorship)
records.design: Systematic review of 9 RCTs of physician-directed domestic violence education
records.population_setting: Postgraduate trainee and practising physicians
records.key_finding: Brief educational interventions for postgraduate trainees improved knowledge but did NOT change screening/identification behaviour; only multifaceted training combined with system-support interventions (reminders, access to victim-support referral pathways, audit/feedback) was associated with increased referrals to domestic-violence support resources.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly supports the T-PHE FAILURE CRITERION's core logic (knowledge/attendance can rise while behavior/outcomes do not) and P5 (referral quality needs system support, not education alone) -- strong analogical evidence that a knowledge-transfer format (education, whether to practitioners or, by extension, premarital couples) does not reliably translate into changed help-seeking or referral behaviour without structural scaffolding.
records.evidence_level: evidence (systematic review of RCTs, provider-training literature analogous to T-PHE's education format)

records.title: Is HIV index testing and partner notification safe for adolescent girls and young women in low- and middle-income countries?
records.first_author: Kalichman SC / or commentary author per abstract
records.journal: Journal of the International AIDS Society
records.design: Commentary / research-agenda-setting article
records.population_setting: Adolescent girls and young women (15-24) in LMICs receiving HIV index-testing/partner-notification services
records.key_finding: Highlights that partner-notification and index-testing approaches proven safe/effective for adult men and cohabiting/married adults have not been adequately studied for younger women with less relationship power, who face higher risk of IPV, stigma, and economic coercion when disclosure is required or facilitated by a health service.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly supports the STOP RULE and P4 (dignity and consent): a global-evidence caution that a well-intentioned disclosure- or joint-engagement-based health protocol can create IPV risk for a less-powerful partner in an unequal relationship if safety is not independently assessed first -- close structural analogy to why T-PHE's stop rule requires joint couple work to halt pending confidential individual assessment.
records.evidence_level: Dr-tier commentary calling for research (not itself a primary study; identifies an evidence gap)

records.title: Family medicine provider and staff identification and response to male patient intimate partner violence perpetration
records.design: Qualitative interview study
records.population_setting: Family medicine providers/staff at two US academic outpatient centers
records.key_finding: Notes that one in five men report lifetime IPV perpetration and two in three male perpetrators seek routine health services, yet family medicine physicians feel unprepared to screen male patients for IPV perpetration due to lack of knowledge/training, despite validated screening tools existing.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Relevant to the bounded-authority-and-referral safeguard and P1 (epistemic humility): supports the plausibility of engaging the higher-power/potentially-perpetrating partner as a decision-control target, while also showing that even trained health professionals report low confidence/readiness to do this work -- a caution for T-PHE's assumption that lay facilitators or premarital counselors can competently perform an analogous function.
records.evidence_level: Dr-tier qualitative evidence (single-country, two-site provider interview study)

records.title: New WHO guidelines on intimate-partner violence
records.design: News item summarizing WHO guideline release
records.population_setting: Global health systems
records.key_finding: Reports the 2013 release of WHO clinical and policy guidelines on responding to intimate partner violence and sexual violence against women, summarizing their call for a first-line, non-judgmental, safety-focused clinical response (the basis of what became the LIVES model) rather than mandatory universal screening.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Secondary reporting corroborating the existence and content of the WHO 2013 guideline (cited directly with its own record below); useful only as a contemporaneous pointer, not as primary evidence -- cited here for completeness but the WHO guideline document itself, not this news item, should be treated as the authoritative source.
records.evidence_level: Non-primary (news/commentary reporting on global guidance; not itself an evidence source)

records.title: Responding to intimate partner violence and sexual violence against women: WHO clinical and policy guidelines
records.journal: WHO (Geneva) -- ISBN 978 92 4 154859 5; WHO IRIS handle https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/85240
records.design: Global clinical and policy guideline
records.population_setting: Global health-system guidance for responding to women subjected to IPV or sexual violence
records.key_finding: Establishes WHO's first-line support principles for clinicians (the basis of the later-named LIVES model: Listen, Inquire about needs, Validate, Enhance safety, Support/refer), recommends against mandatory universal screening in the absence of adequate response systems, and sets minimum requirements (privacy, confidentiality, trained staff, referral pathways) before any clinical inquiry about violence should occur.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Foundational global guidance directly underwriting T-PHE's STOP RULE, the private/confidential channel (P2), and the bounded-authority-and-referral safeguard (P5) -- the LIVES model T-PHE implicitly draws on for first-line response originates here; WHO explicitly conditions any inquiry about violence on a functioning referral system being in place first, which is the same conditionality T-PHE's failure criterion encodes.
records.evidence_level: Global guidance (WHO clinical/policy guideline, cited by ISBN/official URL per PubMed non-indexing of WHO monograph)

records.title: Health care for women subjected to intimate partner violence or sexual violence: a clinical handbook
records.journal: WHO (Geneva) -- WHO reference number WHO/RHR/14.26; WHO IRIS handle https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/136101
records.design: Global clinical practice handbook operationalizing the 2013 WHO guidelines
records.population_setting: Frontline health workers globally, first-line clinical response to women disclosing IPV or sexual violence
records.key_finding: Operationalizes the LIVES first-line support protocol (Listen, Inquire, Validate, Enhance safety, Support) into a step-by-step clinical tool for frontline providers, with explicit guidance on confidentiality, documentation, safety planning, and structured referral rather than passive information provision.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly underwrites the mechanistic content of T-PHE's decision-control/STOP RULE/referral safeguards: this is the primary source specification of the LIVES protocol that Nigeria-trial evidence (PMIDs 41267027, 41151831) tests and that Australian patient-preference evidence (PMID 41330529) validates from the recipient's perspective -- T-PHE should cite this handbook, not only downstream commentary, as the mechanism's origin.
records.evidence_level: Global guidance (WHO clinical handbook, cited by official reference number/URL per PubMed non-indexing of WHO monograph)

gaps_noted: No PubMed-indexed evidence located specific to premarital/pre-nikah education settings combined with IPV screening/response protocols -- all direct LIVES/ARCHES effectiveness evidence (PMIDs 41267027, 41151831, 32460786) comes from antenatal/family-planning clinical encounters, not premarital or religious pre-marriage counselling contexts. This is a genuine evidence gap for T-PHE's specific setting, not merely a search-coverage limitation.

No PubMed-indexed evidence located on IPV screening/response specifically among Muslim or Thai/Southeast Asian couples; the Nigeria trials (Sokoto, Ebonyi) are the closest Muslim-population-adjacent evidence but are clinical, not premarital-education, settings and not Southeast Asian.

No direct evidence found evaluating a 'joint couple education plus individual disclosure channel' hybrid format of the kind T-PHE proposes (P2/P4) -- the closest analogues (LIVES/ARCHES) are individual clinical encounters, not group or joint-couple pedagogical settings, so the STOP RULE's core assumption (joint work can be paused for individual assessment) is supported by clinical first-line-response logic but not tested in an education/curriculum delivery format.

Evidence on harms of screening (adverse effects, loss of privacy, distress) is present (PMID 22565034, 26200817) but almost entirely measured only immediately post-screening, with very limited longer-term harm surveillance across the literature -- relevant to T-PHE's dignity/consent safeguard but not fully answered by current evidence.

The most positive effectiveness evidence for a LIVES/ARCHES-style protocol (PMID 41151831) comes from a single research team's two-state Nigerian trial; independent replication in other settings was not identified in this search.
limits_of_this_search: PubMed-indexed literature only, searched via NCBI E-utilities esearch/efetch with 7 term-based queries (~72 unique candidate PMIDs identified, 20 selected for full-abstract review based on relevance-ranked triage plus 2 WHO global-guidance monographs added by official citation since WHO clinical guideline/handbook monographs are not indexed as journal articles in PubMed). Selection for full-abstract review was investigator-judged for relevance to the ipv-screening-response angle rather than an exhaustive systematic-review protocol (no dual-reviewer screening, no formal risk-of-bias extraction across all 20 records, no grey-literature or non-English search). Search conducted 2026-09-02; results reflect PubMed indexing as of that date.
